power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

marginal.summary_text: You described 6 effects with terms related to 'marginally significant'.

table.text: However, the number and position of the cutoffs can be specified flexibly by the researcher to accommodate various publication processes (e.g., marginally significant studies being more likely to be published than non-significant studies and significant studies more likely to be published than marginally significant studies).

The researcher specifies J -1 cutoffs 0 < a 1 < . . . < a J-1 < 1 that partition the p-value scale into J intervals, such as significant versus marginally significant, versus non-significant p-values, each with its own relative publication probability ω 1, . . ., ω J.
table.formatted: The researcher specifies J -1 cutoffs 0 < a 1 < . . . < a J-1 < 1 that partition the p-value scale into J intervals, such as significant versus marginally significant, versus non-significant p-values, each with its own relative publication probability ω 1 , . . . , ω J.

table.text: The cumulative sum prior ensures ordinality: For instance, with three p-value intervals the prior would be implying that, a priori, interval 1 (e.g., non-significant studies) has an expected relative publication probability of 1/3, interval 2 (e.g., marginally significant studies) has an expected relative publication probability of 2/3, and the last interval (e.g., significant studies) always has a relative publication probability of 1 and serves as the reference category.
For instance, publication probabilities may change at the conventional significance level of p < .05 or at 'marginal significance' p < .10.
table.formatted: For instance, publication probabilities may change at the conventional significance level of p < .05 or at 'marginal significance' p < .10.

table.text: Further, publication bias can operate on a single cutoff (e.g., significant studies are more likely to be published than non-significant studies) or multiple cutoffs (e.g., significant studies are more likely to be published than marginally significant studies, and marginally significant studies are more likely to be published than non-significant studies).

However, in settings with very narrow mixture components and large primary-study sample sizes, it is conceivable that one component contains almost entirely significant results while another contains almost entirely non-significant results.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report:
Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 510 columns across 25 data files.
#### Issues Identified
1 file/column combination has at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = "sim_results.csv", Column = "V1", Issues = "👥 Colliding column names — Column name becomes \"V1\" when special characters are replaced, the ..."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 25 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

#### File paths
**16 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `../run_sim.R` to `../../simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim.R` (in two_step0505.R); `../run_sim.R` to `../../simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim.R` (in two_step052.R); `../run_sim.R` to `../../simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim.R` (in two_step205.R); `../run_sim.R` to `../../simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim.R` (in two_step22.R); `../run_sim_two_sided.R` to `../../simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim_two_sided.R` (in two_sided0505.R); `../run_sim_two_sided.R` to `../../simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim_two_sided.R` (in two_sided052.R); `../run_sim_two_sided.R` to `../../simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim_two_sided.R` (in two_sided205.R); `../run_sim_two_sided.R` to `../../simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim_two_sided.R` (in two_sided22.R); `../run_sim.R` to `../../simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim.R` (in no_bias0505.R); `../run_sim.R` to `../../simulation/simulation2/simulation_scripts/run_sim.R` (in no_bias052.R), and 6 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. **5 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Missing inputs
1 input file the code reads is in the deposit but not usable as named: too large to download, inside an archive, or under a similar name.

#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 36 scripts: 7 ran without error, 3 errored, 3 timed out, 4 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 3 were run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **3 scripts could not be tried, because a file they need was not downloaded**: postprobs_percell.R, visualize_sim_results.R, percell_pb_detection_median.R. **Dependency-unavailable errors**
**4 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable** — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper's code, so it does **not** force the traffic light red.

**Run by another script**
3 scripts are run by another script with `source()`, so they were not run on their own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on their own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Their outcome is part of the sourcing script's outcome.

info.title: Addressing Heterogeneity with Bayesian Meta-Analytic Mixture Modelling

author.affiliation:
Behavioural Science Group

								University of Warwick

text.text: All code and data underlying this manuscript are available at https://osf.io/m2ufv.
text.formatted: All code and data underlying this manuscript are available at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/m2ufv">https://osf.io/m2ufv</ref>.

text.text: The R-package for fitting meta-analytic mixture models is available on CRAN (install.packages("metamixr")) and at https://github.com/MaxMaier42/metamix and additional guidance on the package can be found at https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/.
text.formatted: The R-package for fitting meta-analytic mixture models is available on CRAN (install.packages("metamixr")) and at <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/MaxMaier42/metamix">https://github.com/MaxMaier42/metamix</ref> and additional guidance on the package can be found at <ref type="url" target="https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/">https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/</ref>.

text.text: Meta-analysis is a crucial tool for synthesizing evidence from primary studies.
However, in practice, the application of meta-analysis can be frustrated by various problems, such as high between-study heterogeneity [1] [2] [3] [4] and publication bias [5] [6] [7].
text.formatted: However, in practice, the application of meta-analysis can be frustrated by various problems, such as high between-study heterogeneity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> and publication bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Heterogeneity describes the issue that different primary studies included in a meta-analysis test different true effect sizes.
Heterogeneity can arise for various reasons, such as studies testing different populations or employing different methodologies.

In practice, meta-analysis often focuses strongly on the mean effect size, but when heterogeneity is large, the average effect size in a meta-analysis is usually not very diagnostic of any particular primary study [e.g., 8].
Meta-analysts typically attempt to address heterogeneity by employing moderator analyses; however, even after using appropriate moderators, considerable heterogeneity often remains [4].
text.formatted: Meta-analysts typically attempt to address heterogeneity by employing moderator analyses; however, even after using appropriate moderators, considerable heterogeneity often remains <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Machine learning extensions of moderator analysis, such as meta-CART [9, 10] and MetaForest [11, 12], try to explain additional heterogeneity by relaxing the linearity assumption of meta-regression to identify interactions among many candidate moderators.
text.formatted: Machine learning extensions of moderator analysis, such as meta-CART <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10]</ref> and MetaForest <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12]</ref>, try to explain additional heterogeneity by relaxing the linearity assumption of meta-regression to identify interactions among many candidate moderators.

text.text: However, they still rely on relevant study characteristics being coded and, like conventional moderator analysis, do not account for publication bias.

The issue of unexplained heterogeneity also poses a serious threat to methods that correct for publication bias: these methods usually assume that all effect sizes come from a single normal distribution (random-effects model) or they only model sampling variability (fixed effects model).
If these assumptions are violated, for instance because effects come from a mixture of multiple normal distributions, publication bias correction may be compromised.
These distributional assumptions are often unchecked in empirical meta-analyses and visualizations of model predictions versus data are typically absent.
For many published meta-analyses, it is therefore difficult, or even impossible, for readers to know whether the employed meta-analytic model is adequate for the data.

In fact, a mixture process would give a better account of the data whenever there is an unaccounted-for moderator that partitions studies into groups with distinct effects, which would be the case for categorical moderators, as well as continuous moderators on which the primary studies cluster (e.g., when there are a few common values for the delay between treatment and outcomes).

Given that meta-analyses in psychology usually only evaluate a small number of moderators relative to the space of possible factors that can influence effect sizes, this issue is likely common in practice (see [13] for a review showing high prevalence of non-normal distributions in 54 meta-analyses regarding the effectiveness of psychological treatments).
text.formatted: Given that meta-analyses in psychology usually only evaluate a small number of moderators relative to the space of possible factors that can influence effect sizes, this issue is likely common in practice (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> for a review showing high prevalence of non-normal distributions in 54 meta-analyses regarding the effectiveness of psychological treatments).

text.text: In this article, I develop a new approach to tackling heterogeneity that complements moderator analyses: meta-analytic mixture modelling (MetaMix).
In mixture modelling, clusters of effect sizes (mixture components) are identified in a data-driven way, which can then, in turn, be interpreted by researchers using theory and domain knowledge.

This approach relaxes the assumption that all primary study effects follow a single normal distribution and allows researchers to generate hypotheses about possible moderators that had not been coded in the meta-analysis.
The new method is also combined with publication bias correction methods to allow fitting mixture meta-analysis in the presence of publication bias.

So far, mixture distributions have been used in meta-analysis for two broad purposes: First, mixtures can be used to make inference about the mean effect robust to non-normal heterogeneity, whereby the components themselves are not of interest [e.g., [14] [15] [16] [17] [18] [19].
text.formatted: So far, mixture distributions have been used in meta-analysis for two broad purposes: First, mixtures can be used to make inference about the mean effect robust to non-normal heterogeneity, whereby the components themselves are not of interest [e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: Second, the components can be used to describe the structure of the heterogeneity [e.g., 20, 21] or to separate biased from unbiased studies [22].
text.formatted: Second, the components can be used to describe the structure of the heterogeneity [e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21]</ref> or to separate biased from unbiased studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: MetaMix draws on both approaches: the mixture makes publication bias adjustment robust to non-normal heterogeneity, and the components are additionally made available as a description of the heterogeneity that can generate hypotheses about its sources.

Notably, none of the earlier proposals accounts for publication bias and the mixture process in a single joint model, even though disentangling these two is crucial for making accurate inferences about either in empirical meta-analyses: When data come from a mixture distribution, this may falsely lead to evidence for publication bias, as a publication bias model may be better able to account for the non-normality; conversely, when there is publication bias, a mixture may fit better than a single normal, as it can accommodate skew induced by publication bias, even when the distribution of true effect sizes in fact follows a single normal distribution.
Further, I implement the publication bias corrected mixture meta-analysis in a Bayesian framework in stan [23].

text.text: The Bayesian framework brings a variety of benefits, such as the ability to estimate the posterior probability of different model specifications, update evidence continuously as additional studies become available (avoiding accumulation bias, [24]), and incorporate prior knowledge (see e.g., [25] [26] [27]).

text.text: I evaluate the method in three simulation studies, which show that other publication bias adjustment methods perform poorly when the data are generated by a mixture of normal distributions, while MetaMix performs well.

text.text: Meta-analysts usually model heterogeneity by assuming that the primary study true effect sizes vary according to a single normal distribution, which can be characterized in terms of its mean µ and standard deviation τ (normal-normal or random-effects model).
The observed primary study effect sizes y i (i = 1, . . . , K) are then modelled based on the heterogeneity (τ ) and sampling variation (se i , Equation 1).
text.formatted: The observed primary study effect sizes y i (i = 1, . . . , K) are then modelled based on the heterogeneity (τ ) and sampling variation (se i , Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_0">1</ref>).

text.text: While this approach allows meta-analysts to accommodate normally distributed heterogeneity, the assumption that true effect sizes vary according to a single normal distribution is almost never critically questioned or evaluated in empirical meta-analyses (with a few notable exceptions, which found that a single normal was inappropriate [29, 30]).
text.formatted: While this approach allows meta-analysts to accommodate normally distributed heterogeneity, the assumption that true effect sizes vary according to a single normal distribution is almost never critically questioned or evaluated in empirical meta-analyses (with a few notable exceptions, which found that a single normal was inappropriate <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30]</ref>).

text.text: A few simulation studies have evaluated how well random-effects meta-analysis performs when the normal-normal assumption is violated.
They found that µ is recovered relatively accurately across a range of non-normal distributions [31, 32], while heterogeneity estimates tend to be lower and more variable [33].
text.formatted: They found that µ is recovered relatively accurately across a range of non-normal distributions <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32]</ref>, while heterogeneity estimates tend to be lower and more variable <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: However, when the data are generated from a mixture distribution, it can be questioned whether estimating an overall µ and heterogeneity across two different distributions is theoretically meaningful.

Further, the assumption that the primary study effect sizes follow a single normal distribution also applies to various publication bias adjustment methods that build upon the random-effects model or the more restrictive fixed effects model.
When heterogeneity does not follow a normal distribution, this can distort the inferences from publication bias correction techniques [34].
text.formatted: When heterogeneity does not follow a normal distribution, this can distort the inferences from publication bias correction techniques <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref>.

text.text: We can extend the normal-normal model to a mixture model by allowing the primary study effects to come from M normal distributions, indexed by m = 1, . . . , M , with component-specific means µ m and heterogeneities τ m and mixing weights θ, denoting the proportion of primary studies assigned to each cluster.
Here, I follow a Bayesian implementation of a random-effects model similar to Maier, Bartoš, and Wagenmakers [35].
text.formatted: Here, I follow a Bayesian implementation of a random-effects model similar to Maier, Bartoš, and Wagenmakers <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>.

text.text: Following this paper, I assume a prior of µ ∼ Normal(0, 1) for the mean effect size.
For the heterogeneity parameter, I use τ ∼ Normal + (0, 0.2), which is narrower than in Maier, Bartoš, and Wagenmakers [35].
text.formatted: For the heterogeneity parameter, I use τ ∼ Normal + (0, 0.2), which is narrower than in Maier, Bartoš, and Wagenmakers <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>.

text.text: The reason is that when describing a dataset with a mixture of normals rather than a single normal distribution, one would expect some of the heterogeneity that was captured by τ when fitting a single normal to be captured by the differences in component means instead.
This results in lower heterogeneity within each cluster.
As prior for θ, I use a Dirichlet distribution with α 1...
The Dirichlet distribution is a multivariate extension of the beta distribution to vectors with two or more values that sum to one, whereby the concentration α controls the shape of the distribution.
Setting α 1...
M = 1 implies that a priori each cluster has the same expected mixing weight (i.e., θ m = 1/M).
To account for publication bias, I extend the meta-analytic mixture outlined above using selection models.

Selection models as implemented here model a 'cliff-effect', whereby studies with p-values smaller than specific cutoffs are more likely to be published than studies above these p-value cutoffs [36, 37].
text.formatted: Selection models as implemented here model a 'cliff-effect', whereby studies with p-values smaller than specific cutoffs are more likely to be published than studies above these p-value cutoffs <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37]</ref>.

text.text: Usually, the assumption is that significant studies are more likely to be published than non-significant studies.

However, the number and position of the cutoffs can be specified flexibly by the researcher to accommodate various publication processes (e.g., marginally significant studies being more likely to be published than non-significant studies and significant studies more likely to be published than marginally significant studies).

To account for selection effects, selection models use a weighted likelihood which accommodates the fact that some studies are less likely to be published than others (Equation 3), whereby ω i denotes the relative publication probability of study i, which depends on the p-value interval the study falls into.
text.formatted: To account for selection effects, selection models use a weighted likelihood which accommodates the fact that some studies are less likely to be published than others (Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_3">3</ref>), whereby ω i denotes the relative publication probability of study i, which depends on the p-value interval the study falls into.

text.text: The researcher specifies J -1 cutoffs 0 < a 1 < . . . < a J-1 < 1 that partition the p-value scale into J intervals, such as significant versus marginally significant, versus non-significant p-values, each with its own relative publication probability ω 1 , . . . , ω J.
text.formatted: The researcher specifies J -1 cutoffs 0 < a 1 < . . . < a J-1 < 1 that partition the p-value scale into J intervals, such as significant versus marginally significant, versus non-significant p-values, each with its own relative publication probability ω 1 , . . . , ω J.

text.text: Selection models have been shown to perform relatively well for publication bias correction in simulation studies [35, 38, 39].
text.formatted: Selection models have been shown to perform relatively well for publication bias correction in simulation studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39]</ref>.

text.text: Further, the Bayesian implementation of selection models used here can mitigate typical limitations of frequentist random-effects models, such as convergence difficulties when few primary studies are available in some of the p-value intervals.
Selection models can be incorporated within the mixture framework by modelling a mixture of weighted normal distributions (Equation 4).
text.formatted: Selection models can be incorporated within the mixture framework by modelling a mixture of weighted normal distributions (Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_4">4</ref>).

text.text: As a prior on the relative publication probabilities, I use the cumulative sum of the Dirichlet distribution with α = 1 following Maier, Bartoš, and Wagenmakers [35].
text.formatted: As a prior on the relative publication probabilities, I use the cumulative sum of the Dirichlet distribution with α = 1 following Maier, Bartoš, and Wagenmakers <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>.

text.text: The cumulative sum prior ensures ordinality: For instance, with three p-value intervals the prior would be implying that, a priori, interval 1 (e.g., non-significant studies) has an expected relative publication probability of 1/3, interval 2 (e.g., marginally significant studies) has an expected relative publication probability of 2/3, and the last interval (e.g., significant studies) always has a relative publication probability of 1 and serves as the reference category.

The prior nevertheless allows any combination of publication probabilities consistent with this ordering, so that the data can, for instance, support either no publication bias (all ω ≈ 1) or severe publication bias (small ω 1 and ω 2 ).
To identify the number of mixture components, researchers can compare the probability of the data (marginal likelihood) under models with different assumptions about the data-generating process.
The marginal likelihoods are obtained by integrating the likelihood over the prior distributions for the model parameters: whereby Ω i denotes the entire parameter space under the model H i .
Using the marginal likelihood, one can then obtain the posterior probability of each model given the data using Bayes' theorem.

Analogously, one can obtain the posterior odds from the prior odds using the Bayes factor [BF; [40] [41] [42] [43], which is defined as the probability of the data under two competing hypotheses (or sets of hypotheses, here denoted by i and i).
text.formatted: Analogously, one can obtain the posterior odds from the prior odds using the Bayes factor [BF; <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[43]</ref>, which is defined as the probability of the data under two competing hypotheses (or sets of hypotheses, here denoted by i and i).

text.text: Given that the data could, in theory, have been generated by an infinite number of mixture components, selecting mixture components in this way naturally raises the question of when to stop considering models with additional components.
As a rule of thumb, researchers may stop considering additional models when the data are less likely under a model with K + 1 components than a model with K components.
In addition, due to the Bayesian implementation of the method, the mixture selection can also be guided by expert domain knowledge.

If researchers have prior knowledge that specific numbers of mixture components are more likely, this knowledge can be incorporated by adjusting the prior probability of the different models accordingly.

Model selection via the marginal likelihood can be used to determine not only the appropriate number of mixture components, but also the appropriate specification of the publication process via the selection models.
Meta-analysts need to make a variety of choices when specifying selection models.
For instance, publication probabilities may change at the conventional significance level of p < .05 or at 'marginal significance' p < .10.
text.formatted: For instance, publication probabilities may change at the conventional significance level of p < .05 or at 'marginal significance' p < .10.

text.text: In addition, selection may operate on two-sided tests (equivalent to a one-sided cut-off at p < .025) or one-sided tests.
text.formatted: In addition, selection may operate on two-sided tests (equivalent to a one-sided cut-off at p < .025) or one-sided tests.

text.text: Further, publication bias can operate on a single cutoff (e.g., significant studies are more likely to be published than non-significant studies) or multiple cutoffs (e.g., significant studies are more likely to be published than marginally significant studies, and marginally significant studies are more likely to be published than non-significant studies).

Finally, publication bias may depend on the direction of the effects, such that only significant results in the right direction are selected, or it may be two-sided, such that significant effects are selected for regardless of their direction.

To find a suitable model of the publication process, researchers can compare different selection model specifications via the marginal likelihood in the same way as they can compare different specifications of the mixture process.
I implemented the meta-analytic mixture models using rstan and created an R-package (metamixr) so that researchers without experience coding in stan can fit the models in practice.
Marginal likelihoods are estimated using the bridgesampling R-package [44].

text.text: The next section contains three simulation studies.
First, a small simulation study that validates the implementation of the random-effects mixture model and aims to understand under what conditions the method can identify distinct mixture components.
The second larger simulation study compares the publication bias-adjusted meta-analytic mixture model against a range of alternative methods.
The results show that, while MetaMix performs well, other methods tend to perform poorly when effect sizes follow a mixture of normal distributions.

The third simulation study aims to map out boundary conditions where MetaMix might perform less well: small sample sizes, very unequal cluster allocation, and generating data from a lognormal distribution.

Simulation 2: Publication Bias Adjustment Methods Can Fail When a Mixture Process is Not Modelled
How does a mixture process interact with the presence of publication bias?
Many methods to correct for publication bias assume that the distribution of true effect sizes follows a single normal distribution.
Therefore, inferences from existing methods might be compromised when this normal-normal assumption is violated.

This section extends the previous simulations by including publication bias to 1) validate the implementation of selection models within the meta-analytic mixture models and 2) investigate how existing methods to adjust for publication bias perform when data are assumed to be generated by a mixture.

text.text: Publication Bias.

One benefit of the mixture modelling is that it may improve publication bias detection even when data are not generated from a mixture of normals, as it can flexibly approximate other types of distributions.
Fitting a mixture model indeed considerably improves publication bias detection when data are in fact generated from a log-normal distribution (Figure 8).
text.formatted: Fitting a mixture model indeed considerably improves publication bias detection when data are in fact generated from a log-normal distribution (Figure <ref type="figure">8</ref>).

text.text: MetaMix retains a relatively low false positive rate (albeit a slightly higher one than when data are generated from a mixture of normals), while at the same time reliably detecting publication bias when it is present.
Other methods perform worse than MetaMix and either have high false positive rates or low power to detect publication bias.
This result shows that mixtures are useful as a flexible approximating device to improve inferences about publication bias, even when the data-generating process is not a mixture.

In this section, I illustrate how MetaMix can be used to explore the heterogeneity of nudging.
Nudging describes changing the choice environment (e.g., setting a default option or making one option more salient) in order to steer behaviour without restricting options or altering incentives.
I applied MetaMix to a large meta-analysis on nudging [28], comprising more than 440 effect sizes from more than 200 studies.

For each cluster, I estimated a mixing weight in terms of the proportion of observed studies (i.e., after selection) and a mixing weight in terms of the proportion of all studies (i.e., before selection) in that component.

The pre-selection mixing weight is obtained by adjusting the proportion of observed studies using the average publication probability within each component (i.e., dividing each θ by the average ω within that cluster and renormalising).

Finally, an important consideration when fitting mixture models is the stability of the recovered solution.
Because mixtures are flexible approximating devices, different configurations of components may describe the same data similarly well.
A prerequisite for interpreting mixture components is therefore that the solution is stable under small changes to the data and to the modelling choices.
To assess this, I first refitted each model with 16 chains and random starting values to assess possible posterior multimodality.

Only the two-component selection model was multimodal, and its dominant mode (posterior probability 0.999) reproduced the estimate reported here (see also https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/articles/multimodality.html).
text.formatted: Only the two-component selection model was multimodal, and its dominant mode (posterior probability 0.999) reproduced the estimate reported here (see also <ref type="url" target="https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/articles/multimodality.html">https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/articles/multimodality.html</ref>).

text.text: Second, I refitted the models after randomly removing 10% of the effect sizes and under a range of alternative prior specifications (Appendix F).

The recovered mixture was robust across these variations: the cluster means, mixing weights, and study allocations changed little with the largest effect being that tighter priors on the heterogeneity lead to a larger µ 3 (µ3 = 0.93 [0.42, 1.19] under τ ∼ Normal + (0, 0.1) versus 0.59 [0.18, 1.07] under τ ∼ Normal + (0, 0.5)).

Further, the uncertainty about the number of components remained confined to the choice between three and four clusters; however, the choice between the two did vary across the replicates with some of them strongly favouring a four cluster solution, which splits the first component into two (see Appendix F).
Applications of meta-analysis have long relied on the untested assumption that all effect sizes follow a single normal distribution.
In this paper, I showed that if wrong, this assumption can seriously compromise meta-analytic inferences, in particular in the presence of publication bias.
To mitigate this issue, I propose meta-analytic mixture modelling (MetaMix), which models meta-analytic effect sizes as a mixture of several normal distributions.
I combine Bayesian meta-analytic mixture models with selection models to correct for publication bias and provide them in the metamixr R-package.
In the example provided in this paper, I used existing, coded moderators to characterize the mixture components.

While this is a pragmatic way of interpreting mixture components, especially for reanalyses of secondary data, I anticipate that researchers with domain expertise can consider various additional factors that cannot easily be captured using standard moderator analysis.
In particular, meta-analysts knowledgeable of the primary literature included in the meta-analysis can re-read the studies with highest posterior probability of being in a specific cluster.

This will allow cluster descriptions based on richer theoretical insights than coded moderators, which are often constrained to relatively high-level, easy-to-code variables that apply to all primary studies [72].
text.formatted: This will allow cluster descriptions based on richer theoretical insights than coded moderators, which are often constrained to relatively high-level, easy-to-code variables that apply to all primary studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">[72]</ref>.

text.text: Theoretical knowledge of the domain area under consideration is therefore crucial in meta-analytic mixture modelling in order to interpret the identified clusters.

Further, cluster allocation can be analyzed using machine learning techniques, such as random forest, and associated interpretability techniques, such as permutation importance, to recover the importance of different predictors [73].
text.formatted: Further, cluster allocation can be analyzed using machine learning techniques, such as random forest, and associated interpretability techniques, such as permutation importance, to recover the importance of different predictors <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">[73]</ref>.

text.text: This allows researchers to account for more complex interactions and nonlinear relationships that would be difficult to accommodate in classical moderator analysis.

I expect meta-analytic mixture modelling to be most suitable for relatively large meta-analyses with broader inclusion criteria, as it is more likely that the data indeed arise from a mixture process with distinct components in these types of meta-analyses.

When the distance between cluster means is small relative to the amount of heterogeneity, the number of clusters tends to be underestimated as the distribution of effect sizes is strongly merged (see Figure B1).
text.formatted: When the distance between cluster means is small relative to the amount of heterogeneity, the number of clusters tends to be underestimated as the distribution of effect sizes is strongly merged (see Figure <ref type="figure">B1</ref>).

text.text: However, when the presence of multiple clusters is not detected, applying MetaMix has no downsides compared to applying a random-effects model directly, while it has considerable upsides when multiple clusters are detected.
Similarly, when the primary sample sizes are small, some studies may not be clearly assigned to any one mixture component.
In particular, studies with effect size estimates between component means often have similar probability of belonging to the two closest components.
To mitigate this issue, I recommend focusing on the studies most diagnostic of each cluster when interpreting the mixture components (which will often also be the ones with the largest sample size).
In the example, I visualized studies with a probability larger 50% of corresponding to a cluster.

Because mixtures are highly flexible in how they approximate a distribution, different configurations of components can describe the same data similarly well, and a solution that depends on the particular prior or on a handful of studies should not be interpreted.
Researchers should therefore assess the robustness of a fitted mixture before interpreting it.

Useful checks include refitting the models under alternative prior specifications, refitting after randomly removing a small proportion of studies and examining whether the number of components, the component estimates, and the allocation of studies to components remain stable, as illustrated for the nudging example above.
Importantly, stability of the recovered components is a necessary condition for giving them a substantive interpretation, but it is not a sufficient one, as discussed in the next section.
Like all statistical methods, meta-analytic mixture modelling relies on assumptions.

Although introducing a mixture allows for a more flexible data-generating process than a single normal distribution, it still assumes that effect sizes within each latent cluster are normally distributed, an assumption that is plausible given that the normal distribution is the maximum entropy distribution for a specified mean and variance.
When the underlying distribution is non-normal, a finite mixture of normals usually provides a better approximation of the data-generating process than a single normal.
However, when mixtures are used primarily as approximating devices, researchers should be cautious about assigning substantive or theoretical interpretations to the resulting clusters.

Given that it is difficult to rule out this type of non-normality from the effect sizes alone, a well-fitting mixture does not by itself show that the data-generating process consists of discrete clusters [74].
text.formatted: Given that it is difficult to rule out this type of non-normality from the effect sizes alone, a well-fitting mixture does not by itself show that the data-generating process consists of discrete clusters <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">[74]</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, even when effect sizes genuinely arise from a mixture of normals, the reason for the mixture may not be recoverable from coded study characteristics.

Distinct components need not reflect a single categorical moderator; they could equally result from several interacting or nonlinear moderators, from continuous moderators whose values cluster across studies, or from combinations of methodological characteristics such as measurement, study quality, or sampling differences, many of which may be uncoded or difficult to code.
For these reasons, MetaMix is best regarded as a hypothesis-generating tool for exploring latent heterogeneity structures rather than a direct way of uncovering hidden moderators.
Associations between cluster membership and study characteristics can then be tested in targeted follow-up experiments.

Importantly, these limitations concern only the substantive interpretation of the components: the benefits of mixture modelling for publication bias adjustment do not depend on the components being substantively meaningful, only on the mixture describing the distribution of effect sizes better than a single normal.
Simulation 3 shows that even when data come from a lognormal distribution rather than a mixture of normals, MetaMix improves adjustment for publication bias relative to standard methods.

Latent heterogeneity and publication bias can produce similar patterns in observed effect sizes, such as asymmetry or an excess of significant results [75], raising the question of how to disentangle the two when both are modelled simultaneously.
text.formatted: Latent heterogeneity and publication bias can produce similar patterns in observed effect sizes, such as asymmetry or an excess of significant results <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">[75]</ref>, raising the question of how to disentangle the two when both are modelled simultaneously.

text.text: In MetaMix, identification rests on the different functional forms of the two processes.

Selection is modelled as a step function of the p-value and therefore produces discontinuities in the distribution of z-values at the cutoffs, whereas mixture components are smooth in the effect size and cannot produce such a discontinuity (which is why model fit is best inspected on the z-scale, Figure 10).
text.formatted: Selection is modelled as a step function of the p-value and therefore produces discontinuities in the distribution of z-values at the cutoffs, whereas mixture components are smooth in the effect size and cannot produce such a discontinuity (which is why model fit is best inspected on the z-scale, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_16">10</ref>).

text.text: However, mixture weights and relative publication probabilities can only be separately identified in this way if at least one cluster contains studies spanning different selection probabilities (e.g., both significant and non-significant results).
In practice, this is likely the case most of the time, given that the primary studies within each cluster are more dispersed than the true effect sizes, due to sampling variability.

However, in settings with very narrow mixture components and large primary-study sample sizes, it is conceivable that one component contains almost entirely significant results while another contains almost entirely non-significant results.

In such cases, mixture weights and selection probabilities are not separately identifiable, and strong assumptions for either the selection probabilities or the mixing weights would be required to estimate the model.
This failure mode is visible in Simulation 2, where MetaMix occasionally provided evidence against publication bias under two-sided selection with widely separated, narrow clusters (Figure C1).
text.formatted: This failure mode is visible in Simulation 2, where MetaMix occasionally provided evidence against publication bias under two-sided selection with widely separated, narrow clusters (Figure <ref type="figure">C1</ref>).

text.text: A second identifiability issue concerns the mixture itself.
The ordering constraint on the component means rules out label switching, but the posterior can still be multimodal as different combinations of means and heterogeneities can approximate the data.
When fitting models in a Bayesian framework, multimodality is easily detected if different chains settle in different modes, causing convergence warnings, such as very high R values (see [70]).
text.formatted: When fitting models in a Bayesian framework, multimodality is easily detected if different chains settle in different modes, causing convergence warnings, such as very high R values (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">[70]</ref>).

text.text: Multimodality can be addressed by initialising the chains in each local maximum.
If one maximum clearly dominates (i.e., the data are much more likely under one of the maxima), the inference can be conditioned on that maximum.

If not, uncertainty about the correct mode needs to be transparently stated and propagated to all downstream analyses (e.g., via model-averaging or by reporting results according to both identified modes).
Further, I recommend fitting models with a large number of chains and dispersed starting values to be likely to identify multiple maxima if they are present.

Of course, as with any mixture model, there is no formal guarantee that all modes have been found, since a mode can have a small basin of attraction; running many chains from dispersed starting values makes a consequential omission unlikely but cannot rule it out [76].
text.formatted: Of course, as with any mixture model, there is no formal guarantee that all modes have been found, since a mode can have a small basin of attraction; running many chains from dispersed starting values makes a consequential omission unlikely but cannot rule it out <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">[76]</ref>.

text.text: Detailed guidance on addressing multimodality is available at https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/articles/multimodality.html.
text.formatted: Detailed guidance on addressing multimodality is available at <ref type="url" target="https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/articles/multimodality.html">https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/articles/multimodality.html</ref>.

text.text: In principle, meta-analytic mixture modelling could be combined with various other typical meta-analytic models, such as three-level meta-analysis to account for effect size dependencies (e.g., when some primary studies contribute multiple effect sizes or when multiple treatments share a control condition), or additional models of the publication process, such as methods based on the relationship between effect sizes and standard errors ( [51, 53, 77], but see [78]), or different types of selection models [e.g., 79].
text.formatted: In principle, meta-analytic mixture modelling could be combined with various other typical meta-analytic models, such as three-level meta-analysis to account for effect size dependencies (e.g., when some primary studies contribute multiple effect sizes or when multiple treatments share a control condition), or additional models of the publication process, such as methods based on the relationship between effect sizes and standard errors ( <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[51,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">77]</ref>, but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">[78]</ref>), or different types of selection models [e.g., 79].

text.text: Another promising direction is combining mixture modelling with moderator analysis.
Moderator analysis, in which researchers specify the factors they expect to influence the effect size in advance, can be considered the theory-driven counterpart to meta-analytic mixture modelling.

Combining the two approaches in a single model would allow the mixtures to specifically capture additional patterns in the data that are not yet explained by existing moderators, analogous to fitting a mixture model on the residuals after moderator analysis has been conducted.

This approach would allow researchers to directly test whether, after accounting for suitable moderators, residuals are normally distributed, or additional clusters can be found through mixture modelling.

Finally, the currently implemented approach requires model selection between the different meta-analytic models that can be specified in terms of both the number of mixture components and the different models of publication bias.
To accommodate uncertainty about the data-generating process, researchers can combine meta-analytic mixture modelling with Bayesian model-averaging [80] [81] [82] [83].
text.formatted: To accommodate uncertainty about the data-generating process, researchers can combine meta-analytic mixture modelling with Bayesian model-averaging <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">[80]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">[81]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">[82]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">[83]</ref>.

text.text: Researchers interested in using model-averaging can do so within the current R-package by mixing the posterior distributions from different models (e.g., with different publication processes) weighted by their posterior probability.

Bayesian model-averaging for meta-analytic mixture modelling raises 1) theoretical questions around how to interpret the assignment of primary studies to mixture components when averaging over mixtures with different numbers of components, and 2) practical limitations, as it would vastly increase the time required to fit the models and increase the probability of convergence issues in the larger set of models under consideration for model-averaging.

Ultimately, the value of meta-analysis lies not in producing a single summary estimate, but in helping researchers make sense of the heterogeneity across studies and generate hypotheses about which effects apply for whom and under what conditions.
By allowing meta-analysts to go beyond the traditional normal-normal framework, meta-analytic mixture modelling is an important step toward better addressing heterogeneity in meta-analysis.

text.text: We next compare the robustness of our results when the 4-component fit, which received 42% of the posterior probability, is used for inference (Appendix F).
The 4-mixture split the near-null component into two µ = 0.00 and 0.07, while the components with small and large effects were essentially unchanged (µ = 0.26 and 0.75).
The relative publication probabilities were also similar under the two models (0.08 and 0.21 under four components versus 0.09 and 0.25 under three).

We refitted all models under five alternative prior specifications: an inverse-gamma prior on heterogeneities; a lognormal prior on gaps between adjacent component means, alone and combined with the inverse-gamma prior; and narrower and wider half-normal priors on heterogeneities.
We further assessed robustness to randomly removing 10% of effect sizes ten times (Appendix F).
Across all variations, the one-and two-component models received negligible probability.

Component means and heterogeneities were stable throughout, with the main exception being that tighter priors on the heterogeneity lead to a larger µ 3 , (µ3 = 0.93 [0.42, 1.19] under τ ∼ Normal + (0, 0.1) versus 0.59 [0.18, 1.07] under τ ∼ Normal + (0, 0.5)).
Relative publication probabilities varied little across variations, and the three-or four-component mixture with publication bias was always selected.

We characterised components using the study characteristics of effect sizes with posterior allocation probability above .5 for a given component (Figure 11); restricting to above .75 gave the same picture (Appendix F).

Model Specification, Fitting, and Diagnostics.
All models were fitted with the metamixr R-package (version 0.1.0) using rstan [86]; marginal likelihoods were estimated with bridgesampling [87].
text.formatted: All models were fitted with the metamixr R-package (version 0.1.0) using rstan <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">[86]</ref>; marginal likelihoods were estimated with bridgesampling <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">[87]</ref>.

text.text: We specified the selection model with cutoffs at one-sided p = .5 and p = .975, assuming that effects in the predicted direction are more likely to be published than backfire effects and that significant p-values on two-sided tests are more likely to be published than non-significant p-values.

We used the package's default priors: µ m ∼ Normal(0, 1) on component means, τ m ∼ Normal + (0, 0.2) on heterogeneities, Dirichlet(1, . . . , 1) on mixing weights, and a cumulative Dirichlet(1, . . . , 1) on relative publication probabilities.

For each mixture model, we first ran 16 chains from dispersed starting values to check for multiple posterior modes (see https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/articles/multimodality.html for more details on this approach).
text.formatted: For each mixture model, we first ran 16 chains from dispersed starting values to check for multiple posterior modes (see <ref type="url" target="https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/articles/multimodality.html">https://maxmaier42.github.io/metamix/articles/multimodality.html</ref> for more details on this approach).

text.text: The one-component and three-to five-component models had a single mode.

The two-component selection model had two modes; refitting within each mode showed the data were overwhelmingly more likely under one (posterior probability > 0.99), so we conditioned inference on that mode.

Non-adjusted mixtures under-predicted the number of studies just above the two-sided significance threshold (z = 1.96); selection mixtures reproduced this discontinuity.

Estimates under the selected models.

Under the three-component selection mixture, the first component captured null/near-null effects (µ1 = 0.01, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.04]; τ1 = 0.03, [0.00, 0.05]); the second, small effects (µ2 = 0.21, [0.05, 0.34]; τ² = 0.14, [0.02, 0.24]); the third, larger and more heterogeneous effects (µ3 = 0.69, [0.21, 1.13]; τ3 = 0.34, [0.16, 0.49]).

Relative to significant studies, non-significant studies in the expected direction were published with probability 0.25 [0.15, 0.37], and those in the unexpected direction with probability 0.09 [0.04, 0.18].
